subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT, CRIMINAL CODE, PENITENTIARY ACT AND PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
The Young Offenders Act is the product of a lengthy and detailed examination of juvenile justice. When proclaimed in force some two years ago it saw the repeal of the 75 year old Juvenile Delinquents Act and the introduction of wide ranging reforms in juvenile justice. The principles on which this new legislation is founded reflect our contemporary social values and aspirations rather than those of the Canadian society at the turn of the century.
At the turn of the century it was recognized that children and adults who committed crimes could not be handled in the same manner. It was believed that the young required special treatment consistent with those values. Accordingly, Parliament adopted legislation in 1908 which required the court system to deal with juvenile delinquents as children in need of society's protection, not as criminals requiring punishment. Today we recognize that young people, although they may not be fully adult, are not innocent of their illegal behaviour.
May 22, 1986

In 1982, Parliament in passing the Young Offenders Act declared as a matter of principle that adolescents are responsible for their behaviour and accordingly should be held accountable for those acts in a manner appropriate to their age, maturity and independence.
Not only does the Act give recognition to the principles of responsibility and accountability, it has clearly acknowledged the irrefutable right of society to protection from illegal behaviour. The interests of irresponsible individuals cannot supersede the fundamental rights of society. Society must ensure its integrity and security.
In recognizing the rights of the community and the responsibility of young people, the Act has maintained the balance which is vital to our concept of justice, the commitment to fairness and justice which serves as a hallmark of free and democratic societies. In protecting itself, society must also protect the rights of those individuals who are suspected of crimes and deal sensitively with the special needs and circumstances of youth, youth who are in the process of transition from childhood to full maturity.
When the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin- Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) assumed the responsibilities of Solicitor General of Canada he was already aware that this new legislation had been widely criticized. To examine those criticisms in detail the Minister consulted with Canadians who daily face the challenge of dealing with young people who have offended our laws, as well as with representatives of the communities that are affected by both crime and the criminal justice system. These consultations, and others which he had with his provincial colleagues, confirmed that the principles upon which the Young Offenders Act had been founded are widely supported. In fact, the Solicitor General found that the most adamant critics of this legislation were often equally as firm in their commitment to its basic principles. It is apparent that police, correctional authorities, citizen groups, youth service agencies, and many others, are not opposed to the Act. Rather, they are anxious to ensure that it functions in the way that Parliament intended.
Concerned professionals and citizens have identified a variety of problems and offered suggestions for change. The Solicitor General has been impressed that these actions have been taken with the hope that changes will aid us in achieving the goals of the Act's declaration of principles. It is in this same spirit that the Minister has tabled for the consideration of Hon. Members a series of proposals for amendments, amendments which will serve to enhance the ability of the juvenile justice system to meet demands for public safety and reinforce the values that are fundamental to the high standards for which we strive, including the full recognition of the special needs and circumstances of youth in contemporary communities.
The Solicitor General urges the House to support these amendments. They will modify existing provisions that limit
Young Offenders Act
the ability of law enforcement and justice agencies to achieve the principles of the Act. They will not alter the principles but rather ensure their proper administration.
Among others, the amendments which have been proposed, if adopted, will accomplish the following. The Juvenile Delinquents Act, the predecessor of the Young Offenders Act, established principles which resulted in the juvenile justice system being treated as private and confidential, with no publicity of any aspect of the process permitted. Two provisions in the old Act accomplished this. The first required that all juvenile court hearings be held in camera with no public participation. The second banned the publication of the name or identity of any child who was accused of a crime.
By comparison, the Young Offenders Act has brought the juvenile justice system into public view, opening the courts to public attendance and broad media coverage. However, the Act has continued to prohibit the identification of young people in published reports. In the past year many people have urged that the absolute ban on publication be modified to permit police authorities to seek public assistance in the apprehension of dangerous young people who are at large and a threat to community safety.
In response to this concern the Bill which the Solicitor General has tabled makes provision to permit the police, with the prior authorization of a youth court judge, to release for publication the name of or the identity of a young person who is at large and dangerous to public safety. The amendment also provides young people who are offenders, victims or witnesses appearing in youth court, with an opportunity to request that the court remove the ban on publication in their own cases if they wish to make themselves known publicly.
The amendments will also introduce changes which will enable authorities to deal effectively with young offenders who violate probation orders or other non-custodial dispositions. Currently, the Act relies on a review process to deal with breaches of such court orders, a process which has been found to be generally inadequate. The amendments will streamline the process and allow quick police and correctional intervention by way of arrest and detention where there has been a breach of a non-custodial disposition. The modifications will mean that the juvenile justice system and the adult system will deal with probation breaches in the same way. When young people are involved in street crimes, drug abuse, prostitution and the like, the ability of police to arrest may be a crucial factor in preventing crime and in ultimately helping a young person to achieve a different lifestyle.
The amendments will address concerns that the Act's records provisions are excessively cumbersome and restrictive, thus impeding the adminstration of justice. Specifically, they will ensure that the management of young offenders who are acquitted by reason of insanity will not be hampered by the lack of records. The new records provision will also ensure that police are not prevented from discharging their responsibilities for law enforcement and investigations.

May 22, 1986
Young Offenders Act
There has been a fear that the so-called "Fagins" will be able to commit crimes and avoid prosecution by using children. An amendment to the Criminal Code will ensure that individuals who counsel or aid children under the age of 12 to commit crimes will be liable to criminal prosecution. While there is no evidence that there has been any increase in the incidence of crimes in which children are abused in this way by adults, the Solicitor General wants to ensure that it will not happen. Similarly, proposals to enhance the protection of children who are victims of pornography and prostitution are being examined by the Government.
There is no doubt that the commission of serious crime by young persons, indeed, by people of any age, is a cause of concern to Canadians. In responding to concerns and criticisms of the Young Offenders Act, however, we should note that the majority of young persons dealt with by the Act are not involved in the type of serious criminal activity which has dominated juvenile justice headlines from time to time. There are a number of options open to courts faced with youth who have been charged with such offences.
For the most serious of cases the Act permits the court to transfer charges to the adult court. Where a transfer is ordered, the accused will be subject to all of the penalties that an adult would face, up to and including life imprisonment. This provision, when applied for, has proven to be an effective means of dealing with serious, violent criminal acts, without requiring that we abandon the hope that should motivate juvenile justice.
Generally, the sentencing options available to the youth court appear more than adequate. In the past, 16 and 17-year-olds rarely received sentences of imprisonment longer than two years; and the average sentence was less than five months. Most important, the youth court can exercise considerable flexibility in imposing sentences which reflect the necessity of protecting society. The significant difference is that those sentences will be served in a correctional system which is separate from the adult system and composed of programs designed to respond to the particular needs of young people.
However, in one set of circumstances the provisions of the Act were found to be inappropriate and ineffective. An Ontario court found that a young man who had escaped from prison and committed a series of offences could not be given a proper sentence for the escape and new crimes. The reason was that the Young Offenders Act imposed an upper limit of three years on any aggregate sentence. Obviously, this is contrary to public interest and the Solicitor General is proposing an amendment which would allow courts to impose consecutive sentences for new crimes committed prior to the end of a disposition for an earlier offence. This new measure will result in an aggregate sentence of more than three years in some cases, thereby ensuring that the youth court is able to order appropriate sanctions under certain circumstances. In other cases, the new crimes may justify the transfer of individuals to the ordinary court.
The changes introduced by the Minister will help resolve difficulties in the custody provisions and emphasize that custody is a disposition of last resort intended to enhance the protection of society. Similarly, a general restructuring of the pre-trial detention Sections will resolve procedural problems that have imposed unnecessary burdens on police and in some cases have caused difficulties for young people.
These changes will continue to adhere to the principle that young people and adults should be kept separate and apart from one another in detention and custody. However, the amendments will provide for extended periods of time during which an accused may be kept in the hands of police authorities and will provide for other procedural improvements.
While the Young Offenders Act is sound legislation which enjoys broad support, it is, unfortunately, a law that has been found wanting in several ways. The problems are sufficiently large that a failure to respond to them quickly and seriously will impede the flow and effect of implementation of otherwise praiseworthy concepts. These amendments speak directly to the legislative weaknesses and limitations that have caused frustration among Justice officials and deep concern among citizens across Canada. The Solicitor General hopes that these necessary changes will enjoy speedy passage so that the benefits of the Young Offenders Act can be quickly and more fully enjoyed by Canadian communities.

subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT, CRIMINAL CODE, PENITENTIARY ACT AND PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the Government has finally chosen to call this Bill for second reading. I wish it had done so weeks ago, particularly since the Government is asking us to proceed with it quickly. It is hard to understand why this legislation was not brought forward a month or even longer ago, and I will illustrate that in points I wish to make. Bringing the legislation forward sooner would have allowed for the kind of hearings at committee stage which would assist us in dealing with all of the problems that have been raised during the course of the rather short life of this very important piece of legislation.
I take a particular interest in this legislation and the amendments that are now before the House because, as Hon. Members are aware, I was the Solicitor General who introduced this legislation and defended it on second reading, although I had an excellent Parliamentary Secretary like the Parliamentary Secretary to the present Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty). I came to the House to present the Bill myself and I regret that the Minister is not here himself to do so. However, his place has certainly been very well filled by his Parliamentary Secretary.
I thought that the legislation had a very healthy birth. It was one of the few pieces of legislation that had the unanimous approval on third reading of all Hon. Members of the House of Commons. I considered that to be an excellent launch for an important piece of legislation that represented a major reform of the juvenile justice system. However, very soon that piece of legislation nearly became an orphan. Its difficult period lasted
May 22, 1986

until very recently. I put a certain amount of the blame, though not all of it, for the lack of support the law had at the time it needed it on the present Government.
The former Solicitor General who is now the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) signalled in one way or another that the Bill was back on the table and that its fundamental philosophy, the age limits, the various dispositions provided and virtually every aspect of the Bill were under consideration and that in fact it might be repealed. This had a very troubling effect on the application of this law throughout the country.
For one reason or other a few provinces were urging the Government to take precisely the step indicated, and in the hope the Government would do so they were failing to make some very fundamental decisions that were required so that the Bill would have a healthy introduction into the Canadian criminal justice system. Complementary provincial legislation was needed and some provinces did not pass it because of the signals they received from the first Solicitor General of the Conservative Government. The decisions about which Departments inside the provincial Governments were to take responsibility for the various features of the legislation were not made, again because of the signals that were being received indicating that the legislation might be repealed. Forms that needed to be printed were not being printed. Educational programs that were largely paid for by federal taxpayers were not being delivered, again because of the uncertainty the Government created by indicating that the Bill might be completely abandoned.
I do not want to harp on that. I am glad at the result, that the Government decided that the Bill is essentially a sound one, that its philosophy is correct, that the age limits are proper and that it should be uniform across the country. In other words, after a period of mixed signals and wrong signals the Government is now back on track and wants to make the Young Offenders Act work. I am very happy about that because we in our Party supported the Bill as did the present Government and we want it to work as well.
We turn now to the next chapter in the life of this legislation. What has happened since the Government made the decision that the Bill was basically sound but that some fine tuning was required? No one recognizes more than I that fine tuning of this legislation is required. In fact, when some early decisions were made that put the effectiveness of the Bill in jeopardy, I was perhaps the first person who rose to ask the Solicitor General to quickly bring in amendments to the very legislation that I had taken through the House. I wanted to see the Bill corrected so that the problems that were appearing would be solved, and so that those problems would not continue unduly and thus damage the effectiveness of the legislation. The Government refused to respond in that way. I received a good, smart-alecky put down. I was asked why I was complaining when I was the one who brought the Bill forward. However, that was not my point. My point was that the
Young Offenders Act
legislation existed and the courts and officials were interpreting it in a way that limited its effectiveness. I felt that we should correct it and get on with it.
The Government said it wanted to have a period of consultation so that it could hear from all of the sectors of Canadian society affected by the legislation, and then it would bring in a package of amendments which corrected the Bill and set it on a proper course for the future. If that had been done, I would be agreeing to the Government's timetable. I would be saying, "The Government has consulted, it has put forward amendments, let us get them into law and let us get on with it".
However, I have learned that those consultations have not really taken place and that the amendment package which the Government has brought forward is only a very small part of the story that needs to be told in the House of Commons and in the parliamentary committee before we can really do the job of fine tuning that is required to make this legislation work for the future of the criminal justice system. In saying this, I am recognizing something that I was always prepared to recognize, and that is that the legislation is not perfect and that in the two years it has been working we have learned a lot about its problems.
Why would I challenge the Minister on his claim that full consultations were held? I have been invited to speak on the Young Offenders Act at many conferences around the country. I have spoken to more than 10 groups from one coast to the other and I have done so at the invitation of a great variety of groups. I have spoken to Family Court judges and to assessment officers, the ones who write the assessments that are submitted to a judge when there is the issue of a young person having psychological problems. I have spoken to gatherings of police across the country about how the legislation is going and what the police think should be done to make it work more effectively. I have talked to youth groups about this legislation. For example, I spoke to a very interested group of Boy Scouts in my constituency. They made it a project to study the Act and how it would affect them, their classmates and friends. Like the claim of the Minister, I have tried to get to the grass roots and to all levels of the community affected by this legislation.
As far as the Minister's so-called consultation is concerned he has only talked to the provincial Governments and to the police to a certain extent. Beyond that there has been very little consultation which has been confirmed by some of the groups to whom I have spoken. I asked groups the Minister should not have missed whether they had been given any opportunity to send in an account of their experiences to the Solicitor General, whether they had heard from them and did they know an amendment package was being prepared. It came as news to quite a lot of people. I fault the Minister for limiting his consultation to the provincial Governments, as important as they are, and to some of the leading spokesmen for the police across the country. Those consulations have been

May 22, 1986
Young Offenders Act
pretty good. The amendments that have come forward, which the Parliamentary Secretary described very adequately, covering their concerns are good amendments. By and large we on this side intend to support them.
I am not saying we are going to support all of them or that we do not have some further amendments to make to try to make them more effective. I am sure the Government will accept our amendments in the spirit in which they are intended to improve the legislation, as the Government said, to make sure that the philosophy with which the Government agrees, as we do, is reflected in the way in which the Act is going to work.
Many more aspects of the legislation need to be looked at. I shall not give a long list of them. I will cite just one. Then I will propose a formulation to the Government as to how we might proceed in committee. I hope there will be some favourable response so we can get on with doing what is necessary to the Bill so that it will work.
The one example to which I thought I would refer in some detail is the problem that has arisen with the requirement of Section 22(1) of the Act, namely, the requirement that before treatment is ordered by the court, the young offender having been convicted, has to give his consent to that treatment.
A group of family court judges took me aside, not to discuss a particular case but to discuss the way in which this requirement was going. They told me that it is a very poor idea to ask the young person for his consent. Contrary to the system under the old Act where treatment could be ordered by the judge and a fair number of young people were ordered to have treatment, this is not so under this legislation. The consultation I had was in London, Ontario. The judges said that in some courts the number of cases for which treatment is ordered is down to less than one-tenth of what it was under the old Act.
I know the Parliamentary Secretary and the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) would agree that treatment is a highly desirable disposition for young people in conflict with the law. If there is a recommendation that there be treatment and a capacity of the provincial Government and the court officials to deliver that treatment, surely we ought to do everything we can to encourage the young person to submit to that treatment.
What kind of a handicap or bar does consent present? Young offenders tend to come in groups. They know the court is open. In a lot of cases friends are present. I am told by the judges in the family and the youth courts who deal with these cases that young people do not want to acknowledge in front of their friends that treatment is an appropriate solution. When I was preparing this legislation and the policy issue arose, it seemed to me like a good idea to require the consent of a young person. I thought, and this was the argument of my officials at the time, that if the young person does not consent to the treatment, it is a waste of money and effort. Without a person's consent to being treated, it is obvious that treatment will not work. I agreed with that line of argument, but in light
of the experience with the Act I would like to see a change. I would like to see that provision removed.
I know some argument will be raised about the rights of the individual in connection with this issue of treatment. Should a person not have the right to refuse to have treatment if they do not want it? I think that is a misapplication of the issue of the rights and wrongs or the legal rights of a young person in court. After all, if the judge is going to sentence a young person to be incarcerated for a year or sentence a young person to pay a fine of $1,000, the judge does not ask the young person whether he consents to that disposition. The young person is obliged to accept the disposition whether he likes it or not. It is the judgment and the order of the court. We have, however, built into the law a requirement of consent for treatment. I think that consent should be eliminated. I do not have any hang-up that eliminating it removes some freedom or right a young person has. A young person should not be able to pick and choose among the dispositions that the court, for the person's good, imposes. With the two years of experience we have had to the effect that treatment is being neglected because young people do not agree to it or are unwilling to agree to it in front of their friends, and given the kind of values that gangs of young people in conflict with the law have, I think it is time for us to look at this requirement again.
You may ask how the treatment will work, Mr. Speaker. This is what I asked the judges. How can a treatment work on a young person if that person does not consent to it? Incarceration works because there the person is. A fine works because the bailiff or the sheriff is there to collect the money. The argument is that the treatment will not work if a young person does not consent. Here is where the wisdom of the people working in the field is very useful. They say that eventually young people will want to contribute to the treatment, that young people will want to make the therapy and treatment work. If only you can get them started on it, in most cases or in enough cases they will quickly come to recognize that this is something with which they should play ball, that it is something of which they should try to make a success so as to get themselves into a better value system and into a better lifestyle.
I feel that a mistake was made and experience has shown it. The Minister did not look into this aspect in the course of his consultations, from what I can see, and I think we should not let pass this opportunity to look into measures like this. Perhaps as many as a dozen others might be brought forward, looked at by the committee, witnesses called and the measures included in the amending package. I want to put it to the Government that there was a limited nature to the consula-tions in which it engaged, and let us as a committee hear from all of those who work with the Act, not just provincial Governments, and of course the police but not just the police, to try to iron out a lot of little difficulties, such as the one I have just described.
May 22, 1986

I have limited myself to one example, but if I did speak about another one, I would talk about the review of dispositions problem under Section 33. I talked to people about that in Alberta, Ontario and Quebec. I found a different application in all three provinces, which is normal in a country like Canada, but in some of the provinces it is not working. Provinces are urging us to make an amendment so that an alteration or review of dispositions will not be, as it is becoming in some places in Alberta, for example, a whole new trial of a young person when you are really just seeking a review of dispositions.
I could go on at great length about the kinds of areas not addressed by the Bill that should be addressed by the Bill, but I won't. I wanted to mention the one I have because I am anxious to demonstrate to the Government that there are serious non-partisan reasons for us to slow down in the committee. We should look at a number of concerns and make the amendment package into a really good and useful one.
As an expert on the rules, Mr. Speaker, you know better than any of us that the Opposition will require the Government's support to deal with issues that are not addressed in the series of amendments which we have been given. The chairman of the committee is responsible for ensuring that the committee deals with the measures presented by the Government, and not with measures around it. Therefore, I must ask for the support of the Government for all members of the committee to allow us to widen the scope of our consideration to include all the other questions which I know are important. I think I can convince the Government Members of that if we are given the opportunity to allow these witnesses to speak. Many of these witnesses have not come forward because they did not know that the committee would be holding hearings right now.
That is my position and plea on the Bill. I want to add only one other point. I am not the spokesman for our Party on this legislation. My colleague, the Member for York South- Weston (Mr. Nunziata), is the spokesman but, like the Minister, is not able to be present in the House for this important stage of the legislation. He has some specific concerns about some of the amendments which are actually in the Bill before the House. I do not want to create the impression that the amendments which are there are perfect. I want to hear from the Minister about the provision which can result in a youth court giving sentences of longer than three years. I realize that the background for concern is that in a certain Ontario case a young person drew only a three-year sentence for the crime of murder which was the maximum a youth court could impose.
I do not think that that regrettable result is a bad reflection on the legislation. It was a result of the way the case was handled. The Minister knows about the case and has talked about it. To try to remedy the non-problem by giving the youth court the power, in certain circumstances, to impose longer sentences violates a fundamental principle of the legislation,
Young Offenders Act
that cases of serious criminal activity which require long sentences should not be dealt with in youth court at all. I am afraid that if we put the accused in front of youth courts into the jeopardy of receiving a very long sentence, the youth courts will lose some of the informality and therapeutic dimension which now distinguishes them from adult courts.
After all, if you are a lawyer appearing for a young person who could receive a sentence of seven, eight, or nine years, which is pretty serious, even though you may feel that the young person could benefit from some of the treatment which he would receive in a disposition like that, you would handle the case differently than if you knew that the maximum possible sentence was much less. I think that every aspect of the court procedure would be affected by this measure of providing for very long sentences.
As I said, I am not unwilling to listen to the arguments. I thought the Parliamentary Secretary gave a very good reason for handing down a sentence of longer than three years in the circumstances which he gave. If an individual who is serving a three-year sentence escapes and is brought back to the youth court, he cannot be given any additional time because he is already serving the maximum sentence. Obviously some amendment ought to be introduced to deal with that particular case. However, I would worry about a change in the law which would give a youth court the power to impose such a terrible sentence on a young person. As I said, it might change the way in which the court operates.
I think there are many young people who should receive long sentences for the things that they have done. There are a lot of hardened criminals in the 15 to 17 year old age category. However, the solution within the law, which is quite a good solution, is to transfer that case to adult court. That is almost invariably what happens. It did not happen, although it should have, in the case which the Solicitor General put on the record. I would rather have a solution to that problem than change the whole basis of informality and therapy, which is such a strong, important, and useful characteristic of the youth court as we have continued it under the Young Offenders Act.
I can tell you the good news, Mr. Speaker, that we are only going to have one speaker on second reading of this Bill. I have spoken for my colleague as well as myself. We are anxious to have these amendments passed. We regret that the Bill has been held up like this for no good reason until the last minute. We have been given a short deadline. We do not accept the deadline, but we certainly do accept a limited second reading debate in the hope that the Government and the members of the committee which is to be struck will agree to inviting witnesses to come and tell us how they feel about the whole law rather than just about the particular amendments which the Minister has been persuaded to bring forward at this time.

subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT, CRIMINAL CODE, PENITENTIARY ACT AND PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this very important debate on the Young Offenders Act and the amendments which have been proposed to it by the Government. I had the privilege of

May 22, 1986
Young Offenders Act
participating in the debate at both second and third reading stages of the Young Offenders Act when it was originally proposed as Bill C-61 in 1981 and 1982. I also took part in the proceedings and deliberations of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs before which the then Solicitor General, the Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), appeared to defend the legislation. We had a very thorough opportunity in the course of those hearings to make improvements to the legislation.
I would remind Members of the House that the legislation, as originally presented to the committee, did not make provision for a uniform upper age in the definition of a young offender. I give credit to the Member for York Centre for having brought forward an amendment at an early stage in the committee proceedings to provide for a uniform maximum age of 18.1 think that was an important concept and we supported it. I am pleased that the Government has resisted pressures from some provinces to lower that uniform age to 17 or even to 16. That is particularly important when one considers that in the Provinces of Quebec and Manitoba the maximum age has been 18 for a number of years. Were that maximum age to be lowered, the attempts of those provinces to deal with young people within their jurisdictions under that special regime would have been subverted.
I want to indicate my concern that second reading of this legislation has been delayed until this late date when there is less than a month until the House rises for the summer recess. At the time that the Minister introduced this Bill for first reading in the House I and my colleagues in the Official Opposition indicated that we were prepared to give the Bill careful study but certainly not to delay in any way committee study of the legislation. Having left second reading of the legislation until this late date, it is quite clear that the chances of the Bill being dealt with before the summer recess are very, very slim indeed. It will certainly take some time to give the opportunity which we must give to groups which are active in the field of juvenile justice and should be consulted. We will have to make the time in order to carry out those consultations properly. As I said, Mr. Speaker, that does not mean undue delay. It means doing our job properly as Members of Parliament to give an opportunity and a forum to those groups which are interested in and concerned about this legislation.
I say that partly because it is quite clear that there are a number of concerns which have been raised by these groups and by individuals who are active in the field of juvenile justice which have not been reflected in the amendments which were tabled by the Minister. My colleague, the Member for York Centre, has raised a couple of these concerns. I would like to touch on two or three other areas of concern as well. For example, the Young Offenders Act does not allow for the disposition of a conditional discharge with a probation order. That is a denial of equality to young people because it is available to adults charged under federal statutes, including the Criminal Code. I suggest that in the course of our deliberations we remedy that oversight. As well, we have to look very
seriously at Section 22, the treatment section. Members of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General have received representations from the London family court clinic. They indicated that the provision with respect to consent of a young person before treatment can be ordered is one which has not worked out in practice. We are going to want to hear very careful evidence, not just from that London group but from others who are knowledgeable in this field, particularly those who made submissions to the committee three years ago urging that there be a requirement for consent. My recollection is that the Canadian Psychological Association urged that treatment not be imposed but ordered with the consent of the young person. This provision has not worked in practice. In Ontario, for example, during the first two years of implementation of the Young Offenders Act, only six young people consented to their own treatment needs, which allowed the court to provide them with the most appropriate court intervention. There were only six people. Clearly it was not the intent of the legislation to reduce the number of people who receive treatment. I say "treatment" because that can apply to a whole range of concerns, whether it be learning disabilities or psychological or psychiatric disorders. Those are areas in which proper resources should be devoted, and clearly we are going to have to examine with care the representations made on that particular point.
As well, there have been some court decisions which have brought into question certain provisions of the legislation. For example, in Manitoba a court held that a young person was not able to instruct counsel independently of his or her parents. That decision has been criticized by many people involved in juvenile justice as being unreasonable. An example might be that of a 17-year old charged with impaired driving. To suggest that that individual is not free and able to instruct counsel is not reasonable. Yet there is no provision in this amending legislation to deal with that concern.
Those are some of the areas faced by individuals in the field which have not been addressed by this legislation. Certainly there are others which have been addressed. In some cases we are going to oppose provisions in this Bill vigorously. They are a step backward. For example, while the adoption of the Act in 1982 represented a significant step forward, and it was unanimously approved by all Parties in the House, there were a couple of areas in which we actually moved backward from the days of the old Juvenile Delinquents Act. I want to give a couple of examples because it is precisely in those areas where the Government is suggesting that we further weaken the protection for young people. Under the provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, enacted in 1908, it was impossible and illegal for young people aged 12 or 13 to be locked up with adult prisoners. It was recognized that it would be fundamentally wrong to mix young people at that age with adults in adult prisons. The Young Offenders Act, in Section 7, allowed that to take place. Many witnesses spoke against it. I proposed an amendment to the earlier legislation, but it was defeated. In
May 22, 1986

the Bill now before the House the Government would go even further to dilute the protection available to young people and allow even more of them to come into contact with young adults. We believe that is a regressive step.
As well, the Juvenile Delinquents Act made no provision for transferring young people over the age of 18 from youth correctional facilities to adult jails. The former Minister, in his wisdom, decided to erode those provisions of that Act, so in 1982 he allowed young people originally sentenced as young offenders to be incarcerated in adult jails. That again was a step backward. What the Government is now proposing in this amending Bill is to allow young people to be incarcerated not just in provincial jails but in federal penitentaries. Surely that is not a move we can accept as being a step forward for young people and juvenile justice in this country.
Many of us were relieved when we saw that the Government did not attack the fundamental principle of the legislation. The underlying philosophy of the Young Offenders Act was an enlightened and progressive one. However, as the head of the Criminal Lawyers Association in Toronto, Earl Levy, said, it has its warts. All of us recognize that there is room for improvement. One of the major areas of concern, one which has been of greatest concern to those involved in the field, is the extent to which custodial sentences have greatly increased under the Act. Instead of this Act resulting in a reduction in the number of young people sentenced to custody, whether it be secure or open, we have seen a quite dramatic increase in young people subjected to custodial sentences. In Ontario there was an increase of some 200 per cent.
Another disturbing trend in this legislation is that 16 and 17-year old offenders are getting longer sentences now as young offenders than they would have received in an adult court for the same offence prior to the adoption of the Young Offenders Act. Ironically, legislation intended to reduce the jailing of young people and encourage the provision of alternatives has resulted in a dramatic increase in the number subjected to custodial sentences. One of the amendments proposed by the Government attempts to address this problem, but there is a more serious and fundamental reason for the imposition of these custodial sentences which I would like to address at this point. The scheme of this Act relies very much on provincial co-operation to provide alternatives to incarceration. Those alternatives have simply not been provided. The resources so essential to ensuring that imprisonment is only used as a last resort, in order to ensure that it is effective, have not been made available to the juvenile justice system. When a judge is faced with a young person charged with an offence under the Act, in many cases he has the alternative of either sentencing the person to custodial care or releasing him on probation. That subverts the underlying philosophy and intent of this legislation. That is a very, very serious condemnation of the legislation, one which cannot be addressed directly by this House or the federal Government. Certainly I hope the Government would recognize this problem and work in concert with the provinces and territories in putting additional
Young Offenders Act
resources into alternatives. In too many cases lip service is paid to the rule of custody as a last resort.
Another concern is the very heavy workload of probation officers. This really precludes effective intervention in economic, social and family problems. The underlying concern, however, is that the provinces are not yet offering a range of alternatives aimed at the rehabilitation of young people.
I would note as well that it is essential in this whole area of juvenile justice that we not deal just with the front end of the system, as it were, but that we recognize the essential objective in the area of young people and the law, and young people in conflict with the law, which is to prevent them from coming into conflict with the law. We recognize, as a society, many of the reasons for which young people break the law. Yet we refuse to take action and to deal with those concerns. We refuse to take the preventive steps, which have been identified time and time again, to prevent crime among young people.
There have been many studies done. I would point to one, the study of the Senate Committee on Health, Welfare and Science, which produced a report called Child At Risk. It identified a whole series of steps which we could be taking to prevent crime among young people. It notes, for example, that we have to look right back to the prenatal stage. We have to look at malnutrition of the pregnant mother, the question of intrauterine abuse, the fetal alcohol syndrome, the effect of smoking, the effects of prenatal emotional stress and, of course, diet and possible metabolic disorders.
It is also essential that we examine carefully the resources that are available to deal with learning disabilities. How many young people who are incarcerated in youth custodial facilities are there because no one has detected a learning disability which has driven them, in many cases, to the point of frustration and despair, and finally lashing out and breaking the law?
The Senate study documented very clearly the effects of emotional deprivation. Study after study of adult offenders has shown that, almost without exception, violent offenders have been shuffled between foster homes, have come from broken homes and simply have not had adequate resources when they were young. They were unwanted at birth in many cases, they had frequent placements in infancy, and in almost all cases they graduated from minor offences to major crimes.
There is the whole question of child abuse and how we as a society deal with the sexual and physical abuse of young people. We put totally inadequate resources into identifying child abuse and, having identified it, into treating it. Our resources in the area of child care are grossly inadequate. I know my colleague from Vancouver East, who is in the House today, has been doing an outstanding job in urging the Government to move forward to recognize the implications of a lack of resources in the area of child care for our young people, and ultimately for our juvenile justice system.

May 22, 1986
Young Offenders Act
What about the whole question of violence in the media, violence on television, and violence in video games? 1 am sure that the Speaker has been into these video parlours where young people stand in front of machines and mindlessly shoot away like young Rambos at other human beings. What kind of example does that set? Surely to goodness we have to recognize that these machines, which award bonus points for bonus deaths, should not be encouraged in our society, but rather should be discouraged.
It has been estimated that an average child, during his or her childhood, will see on television some 13,000 or 14,000 deaths, whether it be on cartoons or other television shows. I was shocked recently to see the so-called professional wrestling on television in which big hulks take great pleasure in jumping up and down on one another and battering their heads into submission and beating one another up. What kind of example is that kind of mindless violence to our young people? Is it any wonder that there is a great deal of violence in our society when that is promoted on prime time television?
Finally, we have to look at the underlying economic causes of crime, particularly crime among young people. There is no doubt whatsoever of the link between poverty and juvenile delinquency. I could give many illustrations of this, but I would like to quote from a report called Poor Kids. I cited from this in my speech at second reading of the original Bill on April 15, 1981, as reported on page 9319 of Hansard. It states the following:
To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood of ill health-in infancy, in childhood and throughout your adult life. To be born poor is to face a lesser likelihood that you will finish high school; lesser still that you will attend university.
To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood that you will be judged a delinquent in adolescence and, if so, a greater likelihood that you will be sent to a 'correctional institution'. To be born poor is to have the deck stacked against you at birth, to find life an uphill struggle ever after. To be born poor is unfair to kids.
Truer words have never been spoken. We talk about reducing the level of violent crime among young people, and yet we refuse to attack the causes of that crime. We refuse to recognize that poverty itself is a crime which is being inflicted on the poor of this country.
I want to make particular note of the appalling conditions facing native young people in this country. Members of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General received a letter from Chief Edward Anderson who is the Chief of the Anishinaabe Child and Family Services Inc. in Manitoba. Chief Anderson points out that native young people are disproportionately represented among the ranks of the accused and the incarcerated, both within the juvenile justice system and, of course, in the adult correctional system. Youth correctional facilities, jails and penitentiaries are filled with Indian people. As Chief Anderson points out, very few people relate these disproportionate levels of incarceration to the history of Indian peoples.
The chief notes that during the last four generations Indian children in large numbers have been placed in residential
schools, medical foster homes, group homes, child care institutions and detention centres. It is time that we dealt with realistic alternatives for native young people. Native people, when they come into contact with the justice system have to deal with non-Indian prosecutors, non-Indian lawyers, nonIndian judges, and non-Indian probation officers. Then they are sent away to non-Indian open custody and closed custody institutions.
As Chief Anderson points out, too often these institutions, instead of instilling a sense of respect for law and order in native young people, engender bitterness and hostility. Over the years native people have made numerous requests for more culturally appropriate agencies and services, but so far those requests have been ignored. I believe it is essential that we hear from Chief Anderson and other representatives of native people in Canada to express their concerns about the failure of the justice system towards native people in this country.
There are other areas of concern that have been raised by some of the major groups that are active in the field of juvenile justice. The Canadian Council on Children and Youth, while it has expressed qualified support for the amendments to the Young Offenders Act, has recognized a number of serious concerns. They suggest, for example, that we have to look very seriously at this question of the right of a young person to retain counsel without the intervention of an adult. They have voiced concerns as well about the lack of adequate programming for young people, particularly to deal with the special problems of female offenders.
The John Howard Society has noted a couple of areas of concern with respect to this legislation, while once again supporting, in principle, the over-all thrust of the Bill. They have raised concerns about the provisions that allow consecutive sentences totalling more than three years to accumulate for a young person who commits subsequent offences while still subject to an earlier sentence. The John Howard has expressed concern about the direction to determine more formally which young offender cases should be reviewed to assess the need to try the young person in adult court.
One of the other concerns which I would like to raise, which does not flow directly from the legislation but, rather, from the administration of the legislation, is the practice of at least two provinces, the Province of Ontario and the Province of Nova Scotia, to separate the treatment of young people aged 16 and 17 from the treatment of young people below the age of 16. That has given rise to two standards of justice for young people. Once again, that subverts the principle and the objectives of the legislation.
There are other specific concerns with this legislation that certainly the committee will be dealing with in greater depth once we hold hearings. I want to put the Government on notice very clearly that it must get rid of the very offensive provision in the legislation that would do away with the requirement that a young person must waive in writing his or her right to counsel. According to the present wording of the amending legislation, that basic protection of the rights of young people
May 22, 1986

is being eroded. Certainly that is a provision that we will strenuously resist.
I want to note as well that we are pleased that the Government has brought forward an amendment that would remove the requirement for corroboration of the evidence of a child under the age of 12. Of course, that requirement is not one which applies in the case of adult offenders under the provisions of the Canada Evidence Act. This can and indeed has given rise to problems in the case of a young person who may be charged with an offence against a person under the age of 12. In the absence of any medical or other evidence to corroborate the child's story, the case had to be thrown out of court. For example, if a young child 10 or 11 years old is sexually molested by a teenager, in the absence of any corroborating evidence there is absolutely no opportunity for a conviction in those circumstances. Therefore, I am pleased that the Government has moved forward with an amendment in that area.
Finally, our Party calls on the Government to make adequate resources available to the provinces to ensure that there are real alternatives to incarceration. As I have said, the underlying philosophy of the legislation, which would effectively reduce the number of young people who are incarcerated, has been subverted by provinces that are not prepared to put funds into resources. I reiterate the concern that we must deal with prevention and must not take steps that effectively would undermine the over-all principles of the legislation, which is basically progressive legislation.
There is provision to deal with young offenders who have committed very serious offences, who are not appropriately dealt with under the Young Offenders Act, for transfer to an adult court. In effect, that is the safety valve of the system, and it has not been suggested that this safety valve in any way be removed. Certainly for those young people who are being dealt with under the provisions of the legislation, we do not want to erode the protections.
Another concern about the legislation is that the record keeping provisions, which already were heavily criticized in the previous legislation, are being eroded even further, such as in the area of fingerprints and photographs. We will want to hear evidence on that point as well.
I cannot think of many pieces of legislation that are more important or have a more significant impact on the people of this country than the Young Offenders Act. For decades, indeed hundreds of years, there has been concern about crime among young people. I note that as long ago as 2,000 years, Socrates wrote:
Our youths now love luxury, they have no manners, they have disrespect for authority, disrespect for older people. Children generally are tyrants. They no longer rise when adults enter the room ... They gobble food and tyrannize their teachers.
These concerns have been expressed for a long time. I hope that as Parliament and as a country we recognize that there
Young Offenders Act
can be no task more important than dealing with the priorities of our young people. We in this Party will do everything we can, in the review of these amendments now before the House, to bear that objective in mind. Certainly, we will be proposing amendments in order that that objective can be realized.

speechtext:
ADVISABILITY OF RESTRUCTURING DEBT LOAD Mr. Albert Cooper (Peace River) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Farm Credit Act to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to restructure the debt load of those Canadian farmers, that can be shown to be good managers, and who are facing difficult times because of acts of God or because of extreme economic conditions beyond their control, by:
1. Allowing the Farm Credit Corporation to set aside a portion of the debt held by the Corporation, of proven farm managers, for a set period of time without interest or charges; and
2. Allowing the Farm Credit Corporation to issue loan guarantees to private lenders, provided the private lender writes off a certain minimum amount of the debt it holds and can show the farmer's cash flow is sufficient to meet the new lower payments that result from the lowered principal.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate on my motion, which primarily is designed to deal with one element of the agricultural problem, namely, the whole area of farm debt. I brought this motion forward because the agricultural sector, certainly in the Peace country and, I know, in much of Canada, is facing very serious difficulties. These difficulties can be roughly divided into four causes. First, we recently had a drought in the Peace country and parts of western Canada. The farmers in that region had very poor crops. Their cash flow and income was down, leaving them in a rather naked position.
The federal Government has taken steps in this area and has provided assistance on an acreage basis to many of our farmers in the Peace country. While that aid has been of great assistance, it could have been more. Personally, I would have favoured more assistance, as would the farmers. I know that the Government would have liked to give more assistance. The fact is that the farm community recognizes that the Government has been concerned about these problems and has been taking steps to address them.
The second problem facing farmers in my area and elsewhere is somewhat more difficult because it involves the whole question of international prices. The problem essentially involves the current battle taking place between the European Economic Community and the United States Government over subsidies for agricultural producers. The net result has been that the prices of agricultural commodities have plummeted and, once again, our farmers are faced with a very serious situation. Last year they had the drought. This year they have a problem with prices. Obviously, that paints a picture of a very serious situation for many of our farmers.
The third element which comes to mind is in the area of input costs. Farmers have been faced with rising costs for fertilizers, chemicals and various pieces of equipment and machinery. If we take the whole series of input costs, add it to the international prices and then add it to the drought conditions we experienced last year, the bottom line is a very difficult situation for many of our farmers. In the Peace country, in particular, we find that indeed to be the case.
The fourth element I want to touch on is the issue with which my Private Members' motion really deals, that is, the whole problem of the debt load of many of our farmers. Just a few years ago, in the late 1970s, in my region we found prices were going up quickly. The picture looked very good. As a net result, many of my farmers were asked to expand their operations. There was no shortage of money. The banks and the Farm Credit Corporation were there with funds available. As a result, many of our farmers proceeded to expand their operations, get themselves into a pretty heavy leverage situation with a very high proportion of debt, which I suppose
May 22, 1986

would have been fine if inflation had continued and prices of farmland had continued to grow. The farmers could have continued on with life as it had been with probably not too many serious difficulties. But shortly after 1980, prices took a dramatic downturn. Instead of the prices continuing to climb, as many of our farmers had gambled they would do, prices began to drop. So there were dropping farm prices, high input costs, which were continuing to rise, and international prices which have dropped recently. What we end up with is a very serious situation which threatens many of our farmers.
There is no doubt that the Government has attempted to address the problems we are facing. It has talked about drought assistance. In addition to that, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recently raised the matter of international prices as his topic at the summit meeting, which, of course, was the first time, to my knowledge, that this has ever been done. As a result, we are seeing the whole profile of agriculture raised in this House and in the minds and hearts of Members of Parliament and the Government of Canada. That is encouraging. It is the kind of thing I certainly want to see continue.
The Government as well has tried to deal with the whole matter of input costs. It announced as recently as last month the elimination of the federal sales tax and the excise tax on fuels. That is a buffer for the farmers. Essentially what we have is a Government which is attempting to address a serious problem. It is moving in a number of directions. It is trying to address input costs and international prices. It is trying to deal with acts of God, as it did recently with the drought program. In addition to that, the Government is now looking at the whole business of crop insurance and trying to make adjustments there. We know that those discussions are going on with federal and provincial Governments as well as with the farm community.
That leaves one area about which I am concerned, and that is the whole area of farm debt. That is the reason I came forward with this particular motion. We can address some of the causes and some of the problems, and we can move in different directions with solutions, but, unfortunately, what we are faced with is a large number of farmers who still will be saddled with tremendous debt and in the present circumstances will continue to look at a very bleak future. They will take advantage of some of these programs which will help them to a certain degree. However, as long as they have these massive debts, they will continue to be locked into a very difficult situation and many of them will likely face bankruptcy, receivership or, in some way, be forced off the farm.
What I have presented to the House today is a motion which really has two elements. The first element is essentially a system of set-asides which would kick in in certain cases. I specified those cases. The reason I did so is that I do not think any Government should be involved in looking after a farmer who is not managing his operation properly, who is not doing what he should do or that which is necessary to accomplish a turn-around. But that kind of individual is in the minority. The
Farm Credit Act
truth is that the vast majority of our farmers are good managers. They are hard-working people who are doing the best they can to get their operations going in spite of difficult circumstances. Essentially what I propose is that the Farm Credit Corporation be allowed to set aside a portion of the debt it holds for a particular farmer for a period of time with no interest and without any carrying charges until the farmer's situation improves. That set-aside amount of money then comes back into the formula and the farmer begins again to pay interest and charges and so on which are incurred on his debt.
My motion reads in part that the Government allow the Farm Credit Corporation to restructure the debt load of those Canadian farmers who can be shown to be good managers and who are facing difficult times because of acts of God or because of extreme economic conditions beyond their control. So it is a fairly limited exposure. The reason for that is that it is not the Government's business to get involved with farmers who are not managing their own affairs.
The second element is that many of our farmers do not deal exclusively with the Farm Credit Corporation or do not have knowledge of farm credit but are still faced with the same debt situation. What I have proposed that the House should consider is that the Farm Credit Corporation come up with a form of loan guarantee to allow private lenders to enter into the same sort of arrangement. The reason for this motion is very simple. We face a difficult situation. Farmers are being hit on all fronts. I know the Government is addressing as many of these fronts as it can and it is doing a good job. However, there are still a couple of areas which I would like us to give a hard look, and one of those fundamental areas has to be the whole area of farm debt.
I see my time has expired. I want to make sure that other Hon. Members have a chance to participate in this debate. I am pleased to have had the opportunity to put forward a proposal which I think will provide some help and assistance to many of the farmers in our area and, in fact, across western Canada.

I agree with him; we need the measures which he suggests. The reason we need them is that the Minister of Finance failed so miserably in his Budget to address those selfsame problems.
Hon. Members will probably recall that last year the Leader of the Opposition formed the National Liberal Caucus Task Force on Agriculture. The task force, under the very able leadership of the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), toured the country and made some reports. I would like to share with Hon. Members the report of the Ontario section of the task force wherein it states:
The majority, or 16 farm groups, recommend low and/or stable long term farm loans as the solution to the large farm debt problem. County Federations of Agriculture comprise the majority of the groups that specifically recommend low and stable rates. Another three farm groups recommend that the term of farm loans be required to match the time and length of the associated production period.

We really hope that he will have better luck than we have had at convincing the Government to do what it should have done a long time ago.
Hon. Members will probably remember that in January of 1985 the Department of Finance published a document entitled Tax Issues in Agriculture. Mr. Speaker, first, I must congratulate the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) for recognizing that there is a problem. In the process of recognizing that there is one, he has put his name on record to suggest that the Government do something about it. However, I must also suggest that his is not a serious motion. What he states in his motion is mere rhetoric. He places before the House and before the people of Canada a motion stating in effect that he recognizes the fact that the Government is not doing enough about financing in agriculture. It is not a serious motion in any way at all.
The first part of his motion requires a set-aside provision, which is already part of the Act. This is something which the Farm Credit Corporation already has the right to do. The legislation allows the Farm Credit Corporation to set aside a portion of the debt of proven farm managers held by the corporation for a period of time without interest or charges.
The second part of the Hon. Member's motion is with respect to a write-down provision, which is not a guarantee to farmers and which is something which may not even help them. It is a guarantee to private investors. I must suggest that although the Hon. Member recognizes the problem, he does not recognize that the solution he is putting forward is not a serious one at all and cannot be of value to the farmers of the country.
There are solutions that would help. The Hon. Member's suggestion deals with only one of the causes of the disaster in the farming community and does not really deal with one of the causes at which we must look the hardest. There is no good solution to the problem of farmers other than the establishment of commodity prices which pay the farmer for the cost of production, the land, labour and machinery. Such a parity price structure would make it possible for any farmer with management skills to survive and prosper. The Hon. Member
Farm Credit Act
very carefully worded his resolution to mention farmers who have shown themselves to be good managers.
A parity price structure does, of course, ignore some of the situations which have developed in Canada and the world over the last few years. There is the problem of the world market and of other countries subsidizing products and dumping them on the world market at prices too low to enable a farmer to raise grain. The fact that there is intermittent over-production in the world drives the prices down. These are situations with which we are faced today and with which we should deal.
I wish the Hon. Member luck in sensitizing his caucus colleagues to the problems of the farm structure. As well, I wish him luck in his attempt to stabilize farm input so that farmers will know that we are looking at the structure of farm financing.
If the Government were to guarantee all of those loans, it would cost the Government something like $28 billion, and to some extent, that is what the Hon. Member is suggesting if he is suggesting that all private loans be backed and guaranteed by the Government. With wheat on the Prairies going for $3.50, there is not a bank in the market that will back a loan but will not accept the backing which is suggested here.
The Hon. Member makes good management a condition of the resolution. I wonder if he would want to be the judge of good management. If a farmer who has been farming for five years has not had a crop for five years and consequently goes out of business, does that mean he is a good manager if his neighbour went out of business one year earlier? If he has survived at all, does that mean he is a good manager? How exactly do we decide which farmers are going under because of bad management and which are going under because of other factors over which they have no control?
The Hon. Member is challenging the financial structure of the country. That needs to be done, and I congratulate the Hon. Member for doing so. The financial system skims off the top of the fruits of labour and productivity. The financial system does not contribute to the process of farming. Financial institutions put nothing into farming, no labour, no sweat, no seed, no machinery. They just skim off the top through interest rates. One of the greatest reasons for the elimination of producers in the farming industry right now is the financial structure and the fact that financial institutions are skimming off the top when no one else is getting any profit from farms.
It has always been a mystery to me that we in Canada have allowed a situation to develop which would make money the most important input in the production of grain and food. It is more important than fertilizer, chemicals, seeds, machinery or labour. The most important factor seems to be the money that is lent and the interest on that money. That is the only thing that is guaranteed. The financial structure ensures that the person who lends money will collect his interest on it.
The Hon. Member is shaking up the financial structure by suggesting that there be write-downs, even if the write-downs are to protect the investor and not the farmer, and that there

May 22, 1986
Farm Credit Act
be set-asides as far as interest rates are concerned. Both of these are foreign to the financial structure which this Government and the previous Government have gone to great lengths to protect. Consequently, I hope that he is sensitizing his caucus colleagues to this particular problem.
On March 6, 1986, I asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) about the need for establishing a debt review which would allow for write-downs and eliminations. He promised, as he did before Christmas, after Christmas and at Easter, that he would do so. However, when I suggested that the Bill he was to bring before the legislative committee would have no teeth, he said, "There will be teeth in it, just wait and see. We are doing just that." It seems inadequate to suggest that a motion put before the House at this time will replace the legislation we have been promised four times in the last year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on the motion introduced by my colleague from Peace River (Mr. Cooper) who advocates more flexible financial structures to help farmers.
It is easier to appreciate the gist of this issue if we consider the role played by the Farm Credit Corporation, namely to provide funds and financial advice to farmers to help them build up economically sound businesses. Such has been its role since it was created in 1959. Never in 27 years did the Farm Credit Corporation have to face the kind of challenge now confronting it. Never before have its human and financial resources had to cope with so many help requests from the farming community.
Low prices paid for agricultural products, declining land values, drought conditions, and the impact of American policy and high interest rates all represent as many obstacles to be overcome. The Government is fully aware of the daily struggle of cash-starved Canadian farmers trying to stay in business.
Through the Farm Credit Corporation the Government has approved interest deductions for 5,600 FCC borrowers who were paying between 14 and 16.75 per cent interest on longterm loans. These borrowers were saddled with loans maturing in 25 years or more at unprecedented interest levels. Their interest rates have been lowered to 12.75 per cent over five-year terms.
We have also widened the mandate of the FCC appeal boards so they might review the cases of farmers against whom the FCC was about to initiate liquidation proceedings.

Last September, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced a moratorium on farm foreclosures by the Farm Credit Corporation. That moratorium remains in effect today until programs are in place to assist these financially distressed farmers. One of the programs is already in operation. The commodity-based loan program which was first announced in the February Budget was launched two weeks ago. This is a new approach to farm financing which could help between
4,000	and 5,000 Farm Credit Corporation borrowers who are unable to meet their financial obligations. It will give those in low equity positions another chance to rebuild their businesses. Under the program, loan payments are tied to the farmer's ability to pay and borrowers can pay as little as 6 per cent interest.
The unique feature of these loans is that payments will vary according to what happens to commodity prices. If commodity prices decrease, the principal owed by the farmer will also decrease, as will the payment. If prices increase, greater revenues will be generated and the farmer will be in a better position to handle increased payments. If a borrower stays in this program for the full 10 year term and commodity prices do not improve substantially, the total amount he or she pays will be less than under a conventional mortgage.
If a borrower decides to opt out of the program, the difference between what has been paid under the commodity-based payments and what would have been paid under a conventional mortgage will have to be repaid. However, there is a cap which limits the amount borrowers would have to pay if they choose to opt out of the program or if commodity prices increases sharply during the term of the loan. The cap is 2 per cent above the 10 year rate, which means that at current rates a farmer would never pay more than would be required under a 13 per cent mortgage. In effect, commodity prices would have to increase 7.5 per cent every year for 10 years to reach this cap over the 10 year period of the loan.

It is a program that is not easy to explain, but the Corporation has organized information sessions across the country for groups of producers and representatives of the media. As more people understand how the program works, they will be in a better position to appreciate its merits.
We have received some very encouraging and very positive comments from farmers who initially had some reservations. We think that at least 5,000 borrowers from the Farm Credit Corporation should be able to benefit under this program.

Commodity-based loans will help farmers deal with the risks involved in commodity price fluctuations.
A year ago the corporation introduced another program which was intended to help farmers deal with the risk of interest rate fluctuations. That was the shared risk mortgage program, and it has proven to be very popular with FCC clients. In fact, 20 per cent of the FCC loan approvals during the 1985-86 fiscal year were under this program. Interest rates for the shared risk mortgage are adjusted annually. Increases or decreases are shared equally with the corporation, but clients would never have to pay more than a 2.5 per cent increase during the six year term of the loan. These two programs are indications of the efforts the Farm Credit Corporation is making to provide lending programs that help
May 22, 1986

farmers deal with risk. Two fronts have been addressed: commodity prices and interest rate fluctuations. On other fronts, the questions of crop insurance and stabilization programs have also been addressed.
The Farm Credit Corporation is also monitoring its loans closely so that problems can be identified and solved before they become serious. As well, close to 3,000 borrowers are taking advantage of the advisory services program under which they receive regular financial counselling to help them establish viable farm businesses.

The purpose of these measures is to help FCC borrowers succeed. The effort being made by the FCC is considerable: it is currently carrying more than 17 per cent of these accounts in arrears. Meanwhile, the FCC grants loans for debt consolidation and reschedules others when this can help farmers.
We are aware that the farming community is going through a very difficult period, and the time has come to take a different approach to the problem. That is what we have done, and that is what we intend to go on doing, as long as the situation has not improved. Simplistic answers, such as subsidized interest rates and indiscriminate partial write-offs, would provide only temporary relief for those who really need help and might worsen their position in the longer term.
What we need are long term solutions that will strengthen Canadian agriculture.
