speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apart from the question of debt set-asides, which the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) has introduced today, the FCC has served farmers well. FCC was created to help all farmers, not only those in extreme financial difficulty. I believe the Farm Credit Corporation has done its share to help most of its borrowers to succeed, and FCC pays special attention to the needs of its borrowers in financial difficulty. I know farmers in London-Middlesex on FCC borrowing will be pleased to see the reduction in the interest rate this week for the second time in two months.
As we are speaking today, I have no difficulty in believing that FCC is doing all it can under the circumstances. Over 17 per cent of FCC accounts are in arrears at this moment. It means that those farmers are facing real difficulties. The private lending institutions are reporting that the number of their non-performing loans has increased 100 per cent to 6 per cent.
I think FCC shows a lot of flexibility when it carries a farmer in arrears for a long period of time. When the debt structure of a borrower is not adequate, FCC does not hesitate to help out and reamortize what needs to be and can be reamortized.
There is more than one way to help farmers facing financial difficulty. Not being in a position to allow debt set-asides, FCC had to rely on its ability to manage in a very innovative
Farm Credit Act
and empathetic way. When a farmer has some equity left and when he or she works out a repayment program that is realistic, FCC tries to accommodate that borrower. This approach is successful in many cases. Unfortunately, when it is not, the corporation has to take a greater loss. That is a chance FCC is willing to take to help a farmer on an individual basis.
The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) should know, and he did not say it today, that since last year FCC has come up with very innovative ways to work as a lender in the agricultural field. I am thinking here about the shared risk mortgage that was introduced in April 1985. The objective of this type of loan is to lessen the impact of volatile interest rates on a farming business. It was designed to share the risk equally between the farmer and FCC. It was new, it was different, and it was innovative.
There is a market for this kind of program. It was well targeted and it paid some dividends for farmers. During the 1985-86 fiscal year, more than 20 per cent of all FCC loans were shared risk mortgages. The farm community responded very well.
This month, FCC introduced its commodity-based loan. Here again is an attempt to serve the farm community better by offering a program that meets the specific demands of a well defined group. There was a lot of criticism of this program due to misunderstandings about its real value. It is now on the market. It seems that many farmers think that this program can help them.
FCC employees came up with innovative programs and they are still testing new ideas. Equity financing is one of them. Many groups in the farming community had a chance to offer their opinions in this area. As I said earlier, the Government will make some funds available to FCC so it can work with the debt review boards. This decision is the result of many discussions and consultations with farm organization. In my home province of Ontario, the Grey-Bruce county had debt review board experience.
On December 10, 1984, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) supported the debt review board pilot project that was established in Bruce-Grey counties in Ontario. He fully supported the participation of FCC on this project. In May of last year, the debt review board presented its report. While the experience provided us with a very interesting insight on how such a process could work, it failed to establish a consensus among its participants. The concern of the board was to help farmers stay in business if they thought there was a chance for survival and financial recovery. This exercise was not done in vain. In fact, the report of this pilot project and the discussions the Minister had with FCC's appeal board chairman served as a basis for the introduction of what was announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his February 26 Budget.
The Budget included $65 million this year and $130 million next year for a total of $195 million over two years to help

May 22, 1986
Farm Credit Act
Canadian farmers. We think that this is quite an allocation. It included provisions to allow FCC to launch its innovative commodity-based loan program that will help up to 5,000 Canadian farmers. It also addressed the question of those having to phase out of agriculture to seek alternative employment. This program has been very useful in the farming of tobacco in London-Middlesex.
The Government is committed to introducing legislation to establish farm debt review panels to provide advice and assistance in restructuring farmers' debt. We also think that this will have an effect on private lenders. So far the complaint has been that nothing could be done because FCC would not move and would not accept any compromise. Now it will be different.
FCC has a lot of experience in working with independent groups like the debt review boards. FCC has its own network of appeal boards. Those boards are composed of farmers and they can make recommendations to FCC about specific cases which are presented to them. Working with debt review boards will put FCC on the same footing as other lenders. I think its influence will be positive on the over-all process of debt revision. FCC will be able to accommodate all sorts of recommendations from these boards and set-asides are only part of what can be suggested to lenders. I am sure that the Hon. Member for Peace River will be happy to hear that.
There are also write-offs, debt forgiveness, interest reductions and anything positive that is acceptable to both lenders and borrowers. Debt review boards will greatly help farmers facing insolvency. If there is a realistic and feasible solution, they will try to use it. This is very important because the farmers of the country know that the Government is developing plans and wants to listen to them. They will be looking for voluntary arrangements between farmers and their creditors. The Farm Credit Corporation will lend its full support and expertise to this new process to ensure its success.
I thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for this opportunity to speak today on behalf of the farmers of Canada who know that the Government is providing leadership for them.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. This is a two-part motion, as I was saying. The first part calls for an amendment to the Farm Credit Act to allow the FCC to set aside a portion of the debt held by the corporation, of proven farm managers, for a set period of time without interest or charges.
I have some doubt that this kind of amendment is necessary. Section ll.(l)(e) of the Farm Credit Act provides that the Farm Credit Corporation may:
-make compositions or schemes of arrangement, grant extensions of time, accept other security in substitution for any security held by the Corporation and revise, amend or re-negotiate any mortgage or other agreement;
I think that in those broadly stated objectives, purposes, and powers, the corporation already has the power to do the kind of
May 22, 1986

thing which the Hon. Member for Peace River indicates in his motion he wishes it to be enabled to do. However, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Cabinet have not seen fit to provide, by regulation, the power to carry out that part of the corporation's mandate. That is really what is at issue. In fact, that is what has become the issue throughout the farm financial crisis in Canada for those farmers who are borrowing money from the Farm Credit Corporation. The fact is that the Government has not lived up to promises as expected. It has not provided the services which it promised during the election. It has not put real action behind its words.
We were promised that there would be debt review boards. There was a debt review process in Bruce County and, as a result of that, we discovered that lending institutions could not agree on what sort of debt review process should be followed. As a consequence, nothing has happened. According to the Act, the Minister could provide regulations to enable the corporation to make compositions or schemes of arrangement, grant extensions of time, accept other security in substitution, etc. The Minister prefers, instead, to do nothing.
A very good job has been done of making politics out of the issue. Some 40,000 farmers in Canada are under the gun, being faced with foreclosure or being pushed off the farm. FCC has been instructed by the Minister to put a moratorium on those foreclosures pending the action of the Minister and the Government. In several speeches the Minister promised action on the debt review process. He promised that the legislation would be before the House and dealt with before Christmas. That was in the now famous speech in which he said that it would be good legislation, that it would address the problem, and that it would be legislation with teeth.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) took up the clarion call when he brought down the Budget. He said that it is the intention of the Government, under the Budget, to put before the House a system of debt review panels to handle the problem of farmers facing bankruptcy and to provide for composition of debt, etc. That was part of the budget statement. So we had the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance both reiterating a campaign promise. At the end of April we had the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) jumping into the act with his now famous agricultural statement which included a promise that the legislation would be in place not before Christmas but before June. Today we are debating a motion presented by an equally frustrated Member of Parliament, another private Member of this House, a Member from Peace River who is, as we are, getting a little tired of waiting. I think he hopes that with his motion he might twist the tails of the three very reliable gentlemen I have just mentioned so that we will have legislation in time to act before the end of June.
It is not that the House is overburdened these days. We are going to be running out of business some three-quarters of an hour before the normal time today. However, it is very difficult
Farm Credit Act
to deal with a piece of business that has not yet been drafted and placed before the House. If the Bill is going to be drafted properly to deal with the whole range of financial problems farmers face, it will have to deal with much more than just farmers who have loans from the Farm Credit Corporation. It is going to have to deal with farm loans from all kinds of credit institutions. It is going to have to treat farmers in a manner not too much different from the way it treats the rest of society so that we do not have unnecessary conflict between sectors. It has to be fair and presented in time for a thoughtful response, not only from Parties in the House but from the farmers affected and the lending institutions as well.
This issue has been before the House for the last six or seven years. A couple of Ministers responsible for consumer and corporate affairs were going to include a system of handling debt review for farmers and fishermen as part of the new revised bankruptcy law. An agreement was reached just before the last Parliament ended which seemed to have the acceptance of the financial community and others concerned. However, that legislation has not been reintroduced and I think we would be better served, even though I understand the frustration of the Hon. Member for Peace River, by some real draft legislation presented to the House in time for us to give it the thoughtful consideration it needs so we can act instead of continuing to talk about this particular issue.

Mr. Speaker, my submission in the adjournment debate today arises from a response by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to a question I posed to him on April 28. Before I go into the specific points of dissatisfaction with this response, I think it will be valuable to place on the record the background and subject matter of my question.
Briefly, it concerns the denial of a tax remission to the laid-off workers of the Griffith Mine, particularly those living in the Ear Falls area. The fundamental dissatisfaction those people have lies with what the Government had promised, quite unsolicited, and which is now being left undelivered in this particular case. I would like to quote a couple of statements by the Minister of Finance because I think they are germane to the matter and relevant to a full understanding of it. In the November 8, 1984 Economic Statement, at page 101 of Hansard, the Minister of Finance stated:
The consequences of closures are particularly severe for workers in communities where alternative employment opportunities are limited or simply do not exist.
We intend to offer tax relief for termination benefits in these circumstances and will consult with those affected before determining the precise form of assistance.
Further to that, on November 16, 1984, I directed this question to the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton):
If in fact the mine does close, will the Government ensure that assistance similar to that given to the mines recently closed in Quebec will be given to this area?
The reply by the Minister:
Without question, Mr. Speaker!
Quoting now from the Budget Speech of May 23, 1985, the Minister of Finance reiterates the basis for granting tax remissions in closure situations of isolated communities. At page 5017 of Hansard he said:
Tax relief for severance compensation will be offered on a case-by-case basis, to employees affected by a company closure in isolated communities.
This was essentially a reiteration in a slightly different form of the Minister's previous commitment. Late in March of this year, when in Hamilton in the middle of a media scrum, the Minister was asked by a CBC reporter as to whether the Government was granting the tax remission to the laid-off Griffith Mine workers. The Minister stated, in that most inappropriate forum, that no, the Government had no plan to grant such a remission.
Following that surprising revelation, which went completely contrary to everything that the Minister's officials had communicated to myself and to my office up to that time, I attempted on, I believe, three occasions to get a commitment from the Minister to reconsider that decision, as it apparently was, in light of the facts. I had great difficulty securing that commitment, and, in fact, only yesterday did I secure the commitment from the Minister in a meeting.
The reply of the Minister to a question by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) contained some enlightening statements. The Minister cited Campbell Red Lake Mines as being an employer in the area that could be expected to employ people being laid off at the Griffith Mine. The fact was that, having done a survey of the major employers in the area, we found that Campbell Red Lake Mine was planning to employ, at most, two people in the next year or so.
That indicated to us that the Minister had been misinformed as to the facts. After a question in the House, and after questioning the Minister at committee, he finally did put down the criteria under which he rejected a remission for the housing compensation at Ear Falls. It was in the form of a letter to me, and not in the form of a copy of any policy or regulation formally adopted by his Ministry.
Understandably, people do, in good faith, rely on statements made by Ministers. The people at Red Lake and Ear Falls were very angry about the refusal to grant this submission. They sent an invitation to the Minister to come and see their area and to point out to them where the employment opportunities were. I think they have been as irritated, as I have, by the Minister's refusal on two occasions to answer the particular question as to whether he would accept an invitation, and also by the feeling that misleading information was given concerning employment prospects in the area. That is what we would like an answer to.

speechtext:

May 22, 1986

Mr. Speaker, let there be no misunderstanding about the situation of the Griffith Mine as compared with what happened in the town of Gagnon, and about what the Hon. Member said a moment ago. Member for Kenora-Rainy River certainly knows, was destroyed not by fire, but by bulldozers. subtopic: ROAD SAFETY-SCHOOL BUS EQUIPMENT AND STANDARDS
ROAD SAFETY-SCHOOL BUS EQUIPMENT AND STANDARDS
speechtext:
Last April 8 I asked the Hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski):
What part does the federal Government play with regard to the safety of equipment on school buses which carry Canada's greatest treasure, namely, our girls and boys? Is any co-ordination being carried out leading to uniformity in equipment and operations in the provinces?
The Hon. Minister of Transport replied:
-Transport Canada provides the design, manufacturing and functioning standards for school buses in Canada. There are some 35 standards. They are monitored and inspected on a regular basis by the Transport Canada Road Safety Directorate. As far as provincial safety equipment is concerned, that is coordinated under the CCMTA-
I commend Transport Canada on the standards for design and manufacturing of school buses in Canada. The Canadian system of federal standards for bus construction is the envy of our neighbours in the U.S.A. where standards are set state by state. As a matter of fact, accident data indicates that school buses are the safest means of transporting students to and from school. The latest available Canadian analysis entitled "School Bus Accident Study" concluded that a student is eight times more likely to be injured while travelling to and from school in a vehicle other than a school bus.
The 35 federal safety standards referred to by the Minister include the assurance that the school buses are constructed with increased body joint strength, improved window retention, better fuel system integrity and improved occupant protection.
Today, however, I would like to deal with the other aspect of school buses, namely, their operation and what happens outside of the school bus: things like the best known method of loading and unloading school children, school bus driver
Adjournment Debate
training and optional safety lighting systems that would enhance the safety of school children and the drivers who drive in front of or behind school buses. Every province has its own method of protecting the boys and girls who ride in school buses. In Alberta, school jurisdictions have autonomy in public transportation. Some other provinces have a central authority with a mandate to address school bus safety. Consequently, there is a lack of uniform operating procedures within the provinces. This is in contrast to the United States where there have been several federal initiatives to standardize bus operations and to institute driver training programs.
Standardizing bus operations is at least as important as standardizing bus construction. U.S. accident statistics show that for every child killed as a bus occupant, three children are killed outside of the bus, either by the bus itself or by a passing motorist. Canadian accident data collected by an organization known as "Bus Us Safely" show that on a percentage per capita basis, Canadian school children have twice the fatality rate of their American counterparts.
Our provincial Governments are doing something about this; for instance, in Alberta the Hon. Marvin Moore, Minister of Highways, gave notice in 1985 that while the school bus driver improvement program was voluntary, it would be made mandatory if sufficient numbers of drivers do not receive the training. It is already mandatory in Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and perhaps in other provinces. The Department is examining the proposal of a film to increase the awareness of the student's responsibility while a passenger on a school bus and when leaving a bus.
The penalty for offences relating to school buses varies in Alberta and in other provinces. It is the Government's intention to ensure that the penalties for infractions are realistic. There is also a requirement that a school bus operator, wherever the bus stops to load or unload passengers, must activate the flashing lights, and the only exception to this is in large cities where the matter is under the jurisdiction of the city council. A number of provinces only have the four light system.
While the Canadian Conference of Motor Transport Administrators endeavour to co-ordinate matters, there is a limit to their authority. There is a place for the federal Government to provide leadership by co-ordinating the areas of operations as has been done in the area of construction.
As I said at the beginning, our school buses carry the most valuable cargo in Canada-our boys and girls-and we should go the second mile to make sure that not one of these children is killed or injured unnecessarily.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Valcourt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: ROAD SAFETY-SCHOOL BUS EQUIPMENT AND STANDARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the expression of concern about this important area of safety is appreciated. The opportunity to report on the status of school bus safety is most timely in view of current public interest in this subject.

May 22, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Accident data indicates that school buses are the safest means of transporting students to and from school. The 1978 Transport Canada report entitled "School Bus Accident Study", concluded that a student is eight times more likely to be injured while travelling to or from school in a vehicle other than a school bus.
There are, at present, a total of 35 federal safety standards which are applicable to school buses. New safety standards for school buses were introduced in 1980. These ensure that school buses will be constructed with increased body joint strength, improved window retention, better fuel system integrity and improved occupant protection. Because of the special nature of the passengers, that is the physical size range, the protection of children in an accident is accomplished by passive means and depends on high, padded, energy absorbing seats to provide a safe compartment for the child. It should be noted that the safety standards apply to new school buses at the time of their original manufacture.
The on-road use of the buses comes under provincial jurisdiction and usually encompasses items such as driver training, bus maintenance and loading and unloading procedures. Federal and provincial school bus regulations are coordinated through the Canadian Conference of Motor Transport Administrators. This organization formulates policy recommendations for adoption by the Council of Federal and Provincial Ministers responsible for Transportation and Highway Safety.
The safety of school children while riding a school bus is of the utmost importance. Transport Canada continually reviews and revises, when necessary, any regulations that could improve this safety. The Department is also conducting research programs, including full scale crash tests, to investigate potential means of upgrading the safety of school bus occupants.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-HOLSTEIN RESEARCH PROJECT EXPENDITURES. (B) APPROVAL OF PROJECT
NATIONAL REVENUE-HOLSTEIN RESEARCH PROJECT EXPENDITURES. (B) APPROVAL OF PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 16 I put a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay), asking why the Government of Canada continues spending $10 million through the Scientific Research Tax Credit to Dreamstreet Limited, a group of wealthy Wall Street investors.
This research project has been soundly condemned by the Holstein Friesian Association of Canada which says that it is not acceptable. The University of Guelph has turned it down. I have a letter signed by Dr. Kenneth E. Leslie, the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture Food Dairy Co-ordinator. He reviewed the Dreamstreet Redgen project for determining the physiological differences and profitability of the red and white Holstein 1986. He said:
Generally, the protocol has poorly defined objectives, superficial background documentation, inadequate experimental methods and an ambiguous approach to analysis.
He goes on to say:
The motives of this project clearly extend beyond the objectives of the study and the methods are very suspect.
Beyond that, the Co-ordinator of Research for the Government of Canada has condemned the project as being something from which people would only walk away. The Ontario Minister of Agriculture and Food has also condemned the project as useless. The question is who has put the pressure on the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to cause the Government to continue the spending of $10 million? By some reports it may be as high as $50 million over the next 10 years for this project, which seems to have no scientific benefit. People in the dairy industry are offended. They just cannot believe that at the same time the Government is making cut-backs on scientific research by the Agriculture Canada Research Establishment, it is doling out at least $10 million to a group of wealthy investors, supposedly for some purpose, perhaps to raise operating funds for Dreamstreet International, which seems to be having some financial cash flow problems.
I tried to find out from the Minister of National Revenue who is putting the pressure on the Government to keep this thing going and who put the pressure on the Government to get the project approved in the first place. The information we have is that the project was turned down by the Department at least three or four times before it was finally approved by the Minister last November. There seems to be a great deal of political pressure either from the Minister's Office, or from some place, but the Minister essentially just stonewalled. He said he could not give me the information because of the confidentiality of the Income Tax Act. We are not asking about the financial details. We are asking about the scientific value of this project.
The Canadian dairy industry, especially in southwestern Ontario, is really getting fed up with the way in which the Government is handling this affair. It is doling out millions of dollars for a research project which is of no scientific value, yet it is cutting back on Government-sponsored research. The Standing Committee on Agriculture has decided to proceed with hearings. We hope to subpoena Frank Wood, the head of Dreamstreet, who is obviously running this project, as well as other Government officials. I hope in responding tonight the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to clarify these points.
Why does the Government support this project? Why is it spending millions of dollars to establish the largest dairy herd in Canada, which will be paid for by the taxpayers of Canada and ultimately owned by a group of wealthy investors in New York City? It just does not make sense for our Government to do this. The farmers in southwestern Ontario are very upset when they see these moneys being spent for some purpose, we know not what, other than scientific research and the production of dairy cattle.
It is up to the Parliamentary Secretary to lay it all out, to explain exactly who put the pressure on the Minister to get this
May 22, 1986

project approved originally and who keeps the thing going. Obviously the scientific community and the dairy industry are very unapproving of this project, yet the Government continues to spend taxpayers' money on it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Valcourt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-HOLSTEIN RESEARCH PROJECT EXPENDITURES. (B) APPROVAL OF PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it takes some gall for a Member of the Liberal Party to rise in this House today and criticize the Government for having to apply the SRTCs which have ripped off Canadian taxpayers of hundreds of thousands of dollars. If the farmers of southwestern Ontario are upset about this research, perhaps the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) could tell those people that it was his Party, while in Government, which introduced those SRTCs. That is the short answer to the Hon. Member's question.
The long answer is this. There is no one placing pressure on the Minister. The point is that when we took office, we had to deal with this terrible and incomprehensible device of the Liberal Government.
With respect to research being conducted under the SRTC program, it was not possible to cut off that research and grandfather the program for those conducting legitimate research. The way the Hon. Member speaks, it is as if he wishes to undermine this program. That is what he seems to be saying. The Hon. Member knows full well that provisions of the Income Tax Act preclude the Minister, or anyone in his Department, from talking about individual taxpayers. Therefore I cannot say that what the Hon. Member suggests is in fact happening. It is not a matter in the public domain.
Adjournment Debate
What I can tell the Hon. Member is that under this program which the Liberals devised, and which we had to stop, it was not necessary for taxpayers to seek approval for projects, although they could request an opinion or a binding advance income tax ruling based upon plans prescribed by them. Such requests would be dealt with on an impartial basis between the taxpayer, or his representatives, and the Department. I must stress that the program was structured to encourage research without pre-approval by any ministry.
In the great wisdom of the Liberal Party, it should have foreseen this when we established such a law. To ask today that we put an end to it completely and thereby punish legitimate researchers is something we cannot do.
When the Deputy Minister, Mr. Rogers, appeared before the committee, he explained what had been done in terms of the measures taken to protect Canadians. That includes placing funds in escrow, since these matters will keep cropping up in years to come because research is still being carried out.
The short answer to the question is that there is no one putting pressure on the Minister. We just have to live with this Liberal strategem which has ripped millions of dollars off Canadian taxpayers.
